articles.title: Ashley Cole steps away from England Under-21 coaching role
articles.summary: Chelsea legend Ashley Cole has stepped away from his coaching role with England Under-21s after playing a key role in one of the most successful periods in t...
articles.body:
Chelsea legend Ashley Cole has stepped away from his coaching role with England Under-21s after playing a key role in one of the most successful periods in the Young Lions' recent history, talkSPORT reports.

The former England, Arsenal and Chelsea left-back joined the national team set-up in 2021 and helped them win back-to-back European U21 Championship titles in 2023 and 2025.

Cole was part of Lee Carsley's coaching team when the Irish head coach was appointed interim head coach of the senior side.

He also worked with the Football Association (FA), supporting player development and coaching pathways towards the men's senior team.

Carsley praised Cole for his contribution, highlighting his tactical knowledge and experience at the highest level of the game.

He also pointed to the former defender's influence on the players, saying his top-level career allowed him to provide valuable guidance and inspiration.

"I want to pay tribute to Ashley, who played a major part in our two Euro wins and also had a key role in the current campaign with his tactical and technical knowledge," Carsley said.

"As well as being an important part of our coaching team, he also had a positive, inspirational impact on the players given his own elite experience.

"I am certain he will have even more success in his coaching career whatever the future holds."

Cole's coaching career has already taken him through several clubs and roles.

The Premier League Hall of Famer has worked as an assistant to former England teammates Frank Lampard and Wayne Rooney at Derby County and Birmingham City in the Championship.

He also worked under Lampard at Chelsea and Everton in the Premier League. After several years as an assistant, Cole was appointed head coach of Italian Serie B side Cesena.

The 45-year-old arrived in March on a short-term contract due to run until the end of the season, but he won just one of his eight matches in charge before stepping down.

articles.title: Eliot Shorr-Parks Calls Out the Biggest Problem With Eagles’ New Offense Buzz
articles.summary: Eliot Shorr-Parks calls out the biggest problem with the Philadelphia Eagles’ new offense buzz. Their revamped offense has quickly become one of the biggest...
articles.body:
Eliot Shorr-Parks calls out the biggest problem with the Philadelphia Eagles ' new offense buzz. Their revamped offense has quickly become one of the biggest talking points around the team, however, Parks thinks that the hype is getting a little too far ahead of itself.

He is not questioning what the Eagles can do, however, his concern is that everyone is focusing on the scheme instead of the reason the Eagles have actually been so successful.

Eliot Shorr-Parks Questions the Hype Around Philadelphia Eagles ' New Offense

There is plenty to like about what the Eagles are building offensively; with Jalen Hurts at quarterback, Saquon Barkley in the backfield, and weapons such as DeVonta Smith , the Eagles have the personnel to make any system dangerous.

That is exactly why Parks believes the obsession with the offense itself misses the bigger picture.

"A lot of teams run this offense. A lot of teams run this offense and don't win a lot of games. A lot of teams don't win as many games as the Eagles."

His argument is pretty simple: schemes don't win games by themselves. Players do. Parks pointed out that plenty of NFL teams run variations of the same offensive concepts the Eagles are getting attention for, yet very few consistently produce the kind of winning football the Eagles have.

That distinction matters. Philadelphia is not suddenly dangerous because it discovered a revolutionary offensive blueprint. The reason behind their success is that they have a premier quarterback, a top-notch rushing game, skill players who can make things happen, and an offensive line that can run the system effectively.

However, this could turn out to be even more significant in 2026. All those teams that had to face the Eagles would have spent the entire offseason learning how to stop them.

Once the regular season starts, there will not be any time for anything novel about the offensive scheme.

That is where Parks' criticism becomes more interesting. The Eagles don't need their offense to be revolutionary but need it to be efficient, physical, and adaptable. The Eagles already proved that a well-rounded offense can carry a team deep into January. The new system can add another layer, but it cannot replace the fundamentals that made the Eagles contenders in the first place.

Park's warning, then, is not really an attack on Philadelphia's offense but a reminder that fans and analysts shouldn't confuse offensive innovation with winning football.

The Eagles have plenty of talent. If the new-look offense makes that talent even harder to defend, great. However, ultimately, Parks believes the conversation should return to the same thing that has always mattered in Philadelphia: Can they win football games?

articles.title: Braves might have a major lineup problem that could end their season
articles.summary: This problem for the Braves could be what decides their 2026 season.
articles.body:
The Atlanta Braves just had a brutal stretch of games where they allowed the Philadelphia Phillies to make up significant ground in the NL East.

Heading into games on Wednesday, August 26, the Braves were just 4.5 games up on the Phillies. With a month to go and seven games against the Phillies, that's plenty of time for the Braves to lose their lead.

If that were to happen, it might not be due to the starting rotation, as many fans would believe after the trade deadline. Instead, as Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller highlighted, it could be their lineup, with "too many holes," that causes the team's regression.

Braves' lineup holes could lead to NL East collapse

" Atlanta Braves : Too Many Holes in the Lineup," Miller writes. "During the 45-21 start to the season, the Braves offense was relentless, averaging 5.2 runs per game. But since then, Drake Baldwin , Ronald Acuna Jr. , Ozzie Albies , and especially Dominic Smith have all regressed, while 'Atlanta shortstop' has remained a season-long disaster."

The Braves have averaged just 4.1 runs per game while going 31-34 since their hot start came to a close. A regression from the offense has been a huge reason for the team's struggles lately.

In their last 30 days, Matt Olson is the only qualified hitter with an OPS above .740. Michael Harris has a .738 OPS, and Austin Riley has a .725 OPS.

Eli White has a 1.200 OPS, though he's now with the Boston Red Sox . Mike Yastresemski has an .847 OPS, but he's not played enough to qualify in the last 30 days.

Sean Murphy has a .394 OPS, Dominic Smith has a .588 OPS, Albies a .612, and Baldwin a .624 in the last month. Even Acuna, their superstar outfielder, has just a .647 OPS over the last month.

The Braves' offense has really struggled this season as of late, and it could wind up being the reason why the Braves either lose the NL East lead to the Phillies or get bounced in October.

Unless the offense can start clicking again, which is entirely possible, this offensive regression will remain a major "red flag" for the Braves this season.

articles.title: 49ers head to Las Vegas hoping to get preseason finale vs. Raiders out of the way
articles.summary: With the San Francisco 49ers riddled by injuries, roster decisions to make and a long trip to Australia for their season opener ahead of them, playing the Ra...
articles.body:
Thursday in Las Vegas is just a game the San Francisco 49ers need to get through while looking ahead to resolving major questions about their roster. A quarter of their team is injured. And given the quick turnaround time before the team's trip to Australia, you won't see many familiar faces playing against the Raiders at Allegiant Stadium, according to Kyle Shanahan .

"I don't think you'll see many starters," Shanahan said. "We just don't have enough time as we usually do, so I'll be surprised if any of them are out there. There might be a couple, but it will be closer to how Week 1 (of the preseason) was."

The 49ers fly to Melbourne next Wednesday, arriving a week in advance of their season opener against the Rams, expected to do the exact opposite by arriving the day before.

Shanahan grumbled about the trip in the offseason. He more recently tried to show some excitement for what is the first NFL game to be played in Australia. But with Sunday cuts looming and 23 players on the mend, the impending roster tetris has the head coach focused on trying to get his team to that game on Sept. 10 (Sept. 11 in Australia) in one piece.

"I'm just hoping our team's healthy enough and has the time to get there," Shanahan said. "Those are the challenges of it, just to get there to prepare for it. Guys still trying to recover to get there, the plane flight and things like that. But once you do get there and stuff, we're going to have fun playing in another country and it's going to be a cool atmosphere, things like that. That'll all be good. But right now, I'm just thinking of the challenges of getting our team ready for those three and a half hours."

Those among the 90 players still in camp who do play Thursday are vying for one of 53 spots, or the 17 on the practice squad. But even for the select group of fringe guys that might make the team at that point, final cuts can be misleading, an annual Shanahan reminder. There is no rule against releasing or waiving a player after Sunday.

"I always tell everyone the final 53, all that means is the final 53 that day," Shanahan said. "This is the NFL. You're having to prove this every single day. And even if you feel comfortable because you beat everyone else on the roster, our personnel department is getting a list of people who don't make other rosters to see if they're better than our last guy."

Pakistan captain Babar Azam is hopeful of returning for the second Test against England at Lord's after missing the series opener with a finger injury. articles.title: Ex-Bellator fighter suspended 9 months after testing positive for cocaine metabolites
articles.summary: Ex-Bellator fighter Alejandra Lara won’t be allowed to fight again until 2027
articles.body:
Ex-Bellator fighter Alejandra Lara has been suspended nine months and also fined by the Nevada Athletic Commission after testing positive for a banned substance following her loss in Tuff-N-Uff back in April.

On Wednesday, Deputy Attorney General Mike Detmer presented an adjudication agreement in place after Lara tested positive for benzoylecgonine, which is a metabolite of a "prohibited stimulant." Benzoylecgonine is actually the primary metabolite of cocaine, which is obviously banned at all times for athletes competing in combat sports.

As a result, Lara was handed a nine-month suspension, which runs through Jan. 24, 2027 along with a $412.50 fine, $250.60 in prosecution fees, and she must undergo additional drug testing if she returns to get licensed to fight in Nevada again in the future.

Lara was a very active fighter under the Bellator brand with fights against Illima-Lei Macfarlane, Juliana Velasquez, Kana Watanabe, DeAnna Bennett and many more. She eventually left Bellator, and she's continued competing on the regional scene.

Her most recent fight was a loss to Jaeleen Robledo in Tuff-N-Uff, which is where Lara produced the positive drug test that ended with her facing a nine-month suspension.

articles.title: 15 things to know about Yost Ice Arena, Michigan Hockey’s historic home
articles.summary: Yost Ice Arena is one of college hockey’s most unique venues, but it wasn’t even built for hockey. Here are 15 things to know about Michigan Hockey’s home ar...
articles.body:
Yost Ice Arena feels like it was built for college hockey. The old-school architecture, students practically on top of the ice and noise bouncing around the building make it one of the sport's most recognizable venues.

But what if I told you that Yost wasn't built for hockey at all? The building is more than 100 years old and housed basketball, track and football before Michigan ever put an ice sheet inside.

Like we did with Michigan Stadium and Crisler Center, let's dig into the history of Yost Ice Arena.

Yost opened in 1923 and was dedicated Nov. 10 of that year. The building cost $563,168 and had one of the largest indoor athletic facilities on a college campus at the time. That makes Yost four years older than Michigan Stadium, which opened in 1927.

For its first 50 years, it was Fielding H. Yost Field House. The massive open floor was used for basketball, indoor track and football and baseball practices. The building even featured an indoor running track around the balcony. Hockey wouldn't arrive until decades later.

Like Crisler Center, Michigan's hockey arena is named after a football coach . Fielding H. Yost coached Michigan from 1901-23 and from 1925-26 before serving as athletic director from 1921-41. Yost was also instrumental in developing Michigan's athletic campus, including Michigan Stadium.

Before Crisler, Michigan basketball played at Yost. The first basketball game was on Jan. 11, 1924, when Michigan beat Michigan Agricultural College, now Michigan State, 23-19. The Wolverines would call the building home for more than four decades.

That means Cazzie Russell played his entire Michigan career at Yost. He helped Michigan win three straight Big Ten titles from 1964-66, while the huge crowds he attracted helped create demand for a new basketball arena. That arena became Crisler Center, also known as "The House That Cazzie Built."

Michigan played its final basketball game at Yost on March 11, 1967, losing to Iowa, 83-76. Later that year, the Wolverines moved across the athletic campus into their brand new home at Crisler.

Yost has some serious track history, too. At its first indoor track meet in 1925, Michigan's William DeHart Hubbard tied the world record in the 60-yard dash at 6.2 seconds. Hubbard was also the first Black American athlete to win an individual Olympic gold medal, taking gold in the long jump at the 1924 Paris Olympics.

Basketball and track weren't the only sports to call Yost home. The building also served as an indoor football practice facility. When Bo Schembechler arrived at Michigan, the Wolverines' locker room was on the second floor of Yost.

After basketball moved to Crisler and football shifted to Oosterbaan Field House , Michigan needed a new use for Yost, so baseball coach Don Lund suggested converting the old field house into an ice arena. Michigan did just that in 1973. Fifty years after Yost opened, the hockey team finally moved in.

10. Michigan won its first hockey game there

Michigan hockey officially debuted at Yost on Nov. 2, 1973 against Waterloo Lutheran. The Wolverines won, 6-2, with Gary Morrison scoring twice. More than five decades later, they haven't left.

When hockey arrived, Yost's capacity was 8,100. Today it sits at 5,800, as renovations have traded some of that capacity for improved seating, accessibility and other modern amenities.

12. The attendance record belongs to Michigan State

No surprise here, as a record 8,411 fans packed Yost for Michigan-Michigan State on Jan. 29, 1988. Even better, Michigan State is the opponent for each of the four largest crowds in Yost history.

Keeping a century-old field house functioning as a modern hockey arena takes some work. Michigan lists major renovations in 1973, 1992, 1996, 2001, 2006 and 2012. The 2012 project carried a $14 million budget and brought new seating, accessibility upgrades, improved concourses, loge boxes and a new media level.

14. The rink is named after Red Berenson

The building is Yost, but the ice itself carries another legendary Michigan name. In 2017, Michigan officially named it Red Berenson Rink at Yost Ice Arena. Berenson coached Michigan for 33 seasons, finishing 848-426-92 with national championships in 1996 and 1998, along with 21 conference championships.

Rather than starting over, Michigan has repeatedly renovated Yost while preserving much of what makes it unique. It went from a 1920s fieldhouse to Cazzie Russell's basketball court, a football facility and eventually the home of Michigan hockey.

More than a century after it opened, and more than 50 years after someone decided to put an ice rink inside, it's still going. And somehow, a building that wasn't designed for hockey became one of college hockey's most recognizable homes.

articles.title: Set Point #2: Trying to forget a tumultuous preseason
articles.summary: The first serve of 2026 is in two days.
articles.body:
The players are back on campus, the net has been set up, and the sounds of bouncing balls and diving defensemen can be heard echoing through Welsh-Ryan Arena.

It's been 271 days since Northwestern played a meaningful volleyball game, but that streak will end with just two more tallies. NU heads to Virginia on Friday to kick off its season against George Mason at 5 p.m. CT.

The Patriots went 17-13 last season, including a 3-0 sweep over Rutgers, so the match should provide a baseline of purple-and-white expectations for 2026. A strong start to the season is vital to enter conference play with momentum and experience winning, so there's no room for mistakes against George Mason and the following non-Big Ten games.

With all of that being said, if Friday goes anything like Northwestern's two preseason exhibition matches, the 'Cats are in trouble.

NU traveled to play Milwaukee for its first exhibition game on Aug. 15 and lost three straight sets after stealing away the first one.

The main positive from Northwestern's first time on the court was the potential potency of its attack. Campbell Paris was incredibly impressive in an increased role and had nine kills from the outside. Gabrielle Gerry was another standout on the offensive end as she put down seven kills on eight attempts. Gerry seemed to answer any doubts about her ability as a full-time starter at middle and looked like a sniper when set. Utah State transfer Mara Štiglic also contributed seven kills and the first-year middle combo of Hayley Schaaf and Maya Stillwell had five and four, respectively. NU looked well-rounded and versatile from all three hitting positions as it seemingly always had multiple options.

Yet I said the attack's potential potency for a reason. While there were certainly flashes of an unstoppable, three-pronged attack, mental mistakes and errors held NU back. The 'Cats had 25 hitting errors and hit under 25 percent as a team. Isabella Bullington hit .05 on 20 attempts, and first-year Clara Schramm hit in the negatives with seven errors on 20 attempts. While errors are forgivable in the preseason, Bullington needs to be more efficient and Schramm needs to adjust to the collegiate level if she wants consistent playing time in the regular season.

​Another positive for Northwestern was the setting. While both Wildcat setters are fresh out of the high school ranks, they appeared to handle themselves well. Ellie Stiernagle played more than her counterpart Kaitlyn Bodnar in the match, but the duo ended with 29 and 13 assists, respectively. The setting was not the reason Northwestern lost, and that's a good thing given the massive risk Nollan took on the two diaper dandies.

The main area of concern for Northwestern was the blocking. NU had only four blocks in total and frequently allowed clean attacks to pepper the backrow defense. Blocking was a big problem last season, and it appears to be the Achilles heel of the Wildcats once again.

Northwestern then faced off against Loyola Chicago on Aug. 22. The 'Cats once again lost in four sets after narrowly winning the first, and it was largely the same story.

The offensive repertoire was dazzling at times as Paris and Štiglic led the way with 22 and 17 kills. Bullington added 11 kills, but her nine errors on 43 attempts made for another inefficient day. Gerry saw limited playing time while Kauffman, Schaaf and Stillwell struggled to hit with conviction. The 'Cats hit .189 on the day as their 29 errors plagued them from start to finish.

​Blocking remained an issue for Northwestern throughout the game, and it also struggled from the service line with 10 serving errors. The 'Cats couldn't get out of their own way and simply beat themselves. That will have to change when they face off against better competition.

An important note from the second exhibition game was Stiernagle playing all four sets as the lone setter. She had 44 assists as well as five digs and four kills as she flashed the potential of a complete and polished everyday setter for Northwestern.

Looking at the two exhibition games together, there's a lot to be excited about, but there's even more that needs to be fixed. The errors need to be controlled, the blocking needs to improve mightily and the Wildcats need to walk onto the court against lesser competition knowing that they should win dominantly. I'm not going to overreact to two preseason losses, but it was certainly a week to forget for NU.

Finally, the exhibition matches taught us a lot about Nollan's rotations for 2026. Paris, Štiglic and Bullington should be the main hitting trio as expected, with Schramm looking like the first outside off the bench. Though Gerry didn't play as much in the second exhibition match, her performance against Milwaukee should warrant the first starting middle spot. The second starting middle role appears up for grabs, with Kauffman holding the edge for now over Schaaf. Stiernagle's versatility might have given her full ownership of the setting position as she looked much more comfortable than her fellow first-year Bodnar. Last but not least, there's not much to say about the libero trio of Drew Wright, Gigi Navarrete and Lauren Dignan other than all three will play and all three will play a lot.

Overall, it seems like Nollan more or less knows his rotations for Northwestern's weekend tripleheader, but the 'Cats still need someone to step up to take them to the next level. There's no longer validity to all of the talk of the offseason or even the preseason, as this time next week the season will be in full swing. Northwestern plays George Mason at 5 p.m. CT on Friday, American at 3 p.m. CT on Saturday and Georgetown at 1 p.m. CT on Sunday. The 'Cats are ready to roar.

articles.title: Ja Morant’s Memphis-Area Mansion Sold for Millions

articles.body:
Ja Morant has put his Memphis days behind him, selling his Eads, TN home for $3.2 million, WMC Action News 5's Lydian Coombs reports.

Morant bought the property in 2022, just after securing his five-year, $231 million extension.

"The house spans more than 13,000 square feet and includes multiple living areas intended for both everyday use and larger gatherings," FOX17 WZTV Nashville reported.

"Features described in real estate listings include dedicated entertainment spaces, including a movie theater, salon room, and game rooms, as well as open interiors that prioritize natural light."

Morant bought another home in the same neighborhood for his parents.

Even though the Grizzlies traded Morant on June 29, Morant listed the property for sale on April 3, according to WMC Action News 5 .

Trade rumors were beginning to circulate at the time, and this certainly elevated the belief that his time in a Memphis jersey was coming to an end.

After Ja Morant listed the property, Locked on Grizzlies Podcast Co-Host Joe Mullinax posted a tough pill to swallow for Grizzlies fans on X.

"He wants out, and he's not wrong to feel that way," Mullinax wrote .

"As I said on the show this week. It's time to move on. For all involved, it's best now."

Morant also bought a home in Miami in December, with him seeking a potential move to the Heat . Ja Morant has since listed the house after his arrival in Portland.

articles.title: Nick Smith Jr. Q&A: 'I learned a lot playing with LeBron and Austin Reaves'
articles.summary: Nick Smith Jr. discusses learning from LeBron James and Austin Reaves, his New Balance journey and why staying in the NBA is the real challenge.
articles.body:
Nick Smith Jr. , the 22-year-old guard who spent last season with the Los Angeles Lakers and is currently a free agent, spoke to HoopsHype exclusively at New Balance's 2026 Beantown Elite Experience, where he worked with the campers over several days in Boston.

What was your experience like playing with the Lakers last season?

Nick Smith Jr.: I felt like it was a good experience for me just to go out there and hoop and play with the best players on the Lakers team. Playing with those types of caliber guys, you got to bring it every night. You got to play hard every night, and you just got to stay sharp. And I feel like I learned a lot playing with LeBron and Austin , especially Austin Reaves, because we played the same position and we got the same type of game. So it was a good experience.

What's the best advice you've gotten from Austin Reaves?

NSJ: My guy, AR, is always just telling me to stay patient. Just stay patient with the work. Stay patient with my career and stuff like that. Because I feel like it's a lot of players that are trying to come into this league. It's a lot of players that are trying to stay in the league. So just staying down with the work and making sure I keep my head on straight, for real. That's really about it.

How do you manage the hype and disrespect that come with being a former top recruit now fighting for your spot?

NSJ: You just come in ready to work, whatever they need you to do. When you come into the facility, you just got to put one foot in front of the other and just go to work, to be honest with you. I mean, that was just one of the things me and AR was talking about this last year, just staying patient in my career. I feel like it'll come sooner rather than later, but I just gotta keep a good level head and make sure I just take care of my business.

You probably look at him like a lot of guys do.

NSJ: Yeah, yeah, and he was a lot older than me, so.

What did you take from that 12-game win streak with the South Bay Lakers?

NSJ: Yeah, I think it was 12 or 13. It was fun playing with those guys, man. Being able to be a part of a team that I felt like it was a real brotherhood, a real camaraderie around the team. And I had a good experience playing with those guys. Those guys welcomed me into the team with open arms, and they pretty much let me be me. And I felt like it was a pretty good team. I felt like we could have gone our way if we had played, but yeah, it was a good experience playing with those guys.

What do you take from film sessions, especially with a guy like LeBron in the room?

NSJ: I mean, everybody's pretty much seen it all. I just think that the level of sharpness and the level of the adjustments players make is kind of different, especially LeBron. Like if LeBron says something, that's pretty much what goes on. Like, you know what I'm saying? And he watched pretty much every game. He's the OG of the game. So I don't know. He's just LeBron, man. You've got to be around him just to understand what he's talking about.

What was the most shocking thing you discovered when you first got to the NBA?

NSJ: I didn't know how much money NBA players make. Like, as someone that's in the league, I remember one time I looked at my check, and I'm like, "Dang, that's a pretty good check," you know what I'm saying? Then I looked at LaMelo's check, and I'm like, "Jesus Christ, boy. Golly." [Laughs] You know what I'm saying? So it's different. I mean, the work is still the same. The competitiveness is still the same. It's just basketball at the end of the day. But I'll probably just say that, for real.

What's your experience been like over the last couple of days with the kids here?

NSJ: It's been good, especially being a part of the camp with the campers. And I feel like I was here not too long ago. But just to see them compete against each other and stuff like that and interact with each other, it brings me back home, to be honest with you. And it's just a great opportunity for me to come out here and help out.

Has anything surprised or stood out to you from the campers?

NSJ: Not really. They got a lot of skill, and they were way bigger than what we were when we were kids. But it's a lot of skill out here, and they got a lot of people telling them some good things, or what they need to hear, to go to the next level and stuff like that. So, no, it's been good. I feel like it's been a good experience for them.

What stuck out to you that you never would have expected coming in?

NSJ: The facility. The facility is nice, it's done nicely. I wasn't here last year, but yeah, I mean, I'll probably be back out here for sure, just to be back in the facility.

What do you think of the P350 shoe so far?

NSJ: P350s? It's a good shoe. I'm still trying to work my way into them, I got to break them in. But it's a good shoe. I got to put some more experience in them for sure, put some more work in. It takes time for me to get into any shoe. That's just how my body is.

What drew you to New Balance during your pre-draft process?

NSJ: Yeah, I wasn't like, well, I was seeing Rich Paul wear a lot of New Balances, stuff like that. So having his whole team around, when I was going through the pre-draft, it was kind of hard not to wear New Balances because everybody around was wearing New Balances. So I kind of wanted to be a part of the new wave.

articles.summary: GARY, Ind. (Courtesy of Sioux City Explorers) – Sioux City (42-46) dropped a 5–3 decision to Gary SouthShore (37-51) on Wednesday afternoon. Manager Steve Mo...
articles.body:
GARY, Ind. (Courtesy of Sioux City Explorers) - Sioux City (42-46) dropped a 5–3 decision to Gary SouthShore (37-51) on Wednesday afternoon.

Manager Steve Montgomery summed up the loss, "Didn't execute offensively, didn't get much with runners in scoring position."

The RailCats jumped out to a 3–0 lead in the first inning before the Explorers battled back to tie it in the third.

Alberto Osuna started the comeback with a solo homer in the second, becoming the 12th player in Explorers history to hit at least 17 home runs in a season. Braulio Vásquez then brought home Austin Davis with an infield single, and another run scored on a groundout to tie the game at 3–3.

Gary SouthShore regained the lead in the bottom of the third on a Kevin Watson Jr. home run.

Joe Suozzi added an insurance run with a sacrifice fly in the eighth, making it 5–3.

Sioux City mounted one final threat in the ninth, loading the bases with the tying run at second, but Zac Vooletich grounded out to end the game.

Sioux City finishes the three‑game series at Gary SouthShore on Thursday at 6:45 p.m., with pregame coverage beginning at 6:15 p.m. on KSCJ 94.9 FM and 1360 AM . Fans can also watch every American Association game this season on the league's streaming platform at aabaseball.tv . Tickets for all remaining games are available now by calling the Explorers front office at 712-277-WINS or online at xsbaseball.com.

Alberto Osuna is 23-for-52 in his last 13 games and a 13 game hitting streak. (.442) He has six of the 13 games with at least two hits.

Austin Davis stole one base giving him 69 on the season. He is two away from tying for the American Association single season record.

Sioux City is 2-6 against Gary SouthShore this season.

Sioux City stole three bases giving the team 252 for the season the second straight year they have taken at least 250.

articles.title: Kwan and Bazzana lift streaking Guardians to 4-3 comeback win over Angels
articles.summary: Steven Kwan hit a tying double in the ninth inning, Travis Bazzana followed with a sacrifice fly and the Cleveland Guardians rallied past the Los Angeles Ang...
articles.body:
ANAHEIM, Calif. (AP) — Steven Kwan hit a tying double in the ninth inning, Travis Bazzana followed with a sacrifice fly and the Cleveland Guardians rallied past the Los Angeles Angels 4-3 on Wednesday for their seventh straight victory.

Hunter Gaddis (2-3) retired the final two batters in the eighth to earn the win. Erik Sabrowski worked a scoreless ninth for his second major league save and first since 2024.

With a runner on second, Sabrowski struck out pinch-hitter Travis d'Arnaud and got pinch-hitter Oswald Peraza to pop up to second as Cleveland completed a three-game sweep.

Chase DeLauter , slowed this week by left hamstring tightness, sparked the winning rally with a one-out single off reliever Ryan Watson (1-1) in the ninth.

Petey Halpin ran for DeLauter and went to second on Brayan Rocchio 's single. Kwan roped a ground-rule double to right field for a 3-all tie, and Bazzana's sac fly sent the Angels to their 10th loss this season when leading after eight innings.

Los Angeles starter Grayson Rodriguez gave up one run and seven hits in 5 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking one. Guardians starter Joey Cantillo allowed two hits in six innings but issued a career-high seven walks and committed a first-inning error that led to a run.

Zach Neto led off the bottom of the first with a single and scored when Cantillo fielded Vaughn Grissom 's one-out dribbler and threw the ball into right field.

The Angels extended the lead to 3-0 in the second when Cantillo walked the bases loaded with one out, hit Neto with a pitch to force in a run, and Mike Trout added a sacrifice fly.

Cleveland cut it to 3-1 in the fifth when Rocchio doubled, went to third on Kwan's groundout and scored on Bazzana's sacrifice fly. The Guardians pulled to 3-2 in the eighth when Bazzana bunted for a single, Jo Adell walked and Nathaniel Lowe flared an RBI single to left-center.

Guardians: RHP Tanner Bibee (5-13, 3.97 ERA) starts Friday night in Kansas City .

Angels: LHP Reid Detmers (4-8, 3.62 ERA) faces Phillies RHP Andrew Painter (3-8, 6.04) on Friday night in Anaheim.
